key_terms.meaning: Motion on a straight line; position x(t) gives v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt = d²x/dt².
a = constant, so v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as, where u is initial velocity and s displacement.
a changes with t, v or x; use a = dv/dt or a = v dv/dx and integrate.
a_t = dv/dt; it changes the speed along the tangent to the path.
a_n = v²/ρ toward the centre of curvature; ρ is the radius of curvature; it changes direction.
v_r = dr/dt, v_θ = r dθ/dt; a_r = d²r/dt² − r(dθ/dt)², a_θ = r d²θ/dt² + 2(dr/dt)(dθ/dt).
Motion under gravity alone; horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is −g.
T = 2u sin θ / g for level ground, where u is launch speed and θ launch angle.
R = u² sin 2θ / g for level ground; maximum at θ = 45°.
v_A = v_B + v_A/B; the velocity of A equals that of frame B plus the velocity of A relative to B.
Relation from a taut string or contact that ties speeds or accelerations, e.g. equal speeds along an inextensible string.
A frame in which Newton's first law holds; Newton's second law F = ma is valid.
F + (−ma) = 0; the inertia force −ma turns a dynamics equation into an equilibrium equation.
W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu², where u and v are initial and final speeds.
A force whose work is path-independent; it has potential energy U with F = −dU/dx in one dimension.
Energy stored by position in a conservative field; U = mgh near Earth and U = ½kx² for a spring.
J = ∫F dt = Δp; force integrated over time equals change in momentum.
p = mv; mass times velocity, a vector.
e = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach along the line of impact; 0 ≤ e ≤ 1.
The common normal at the contact point during impact; momentum is conserved along it.

takeaways: Differentiation links position, velocity and acceleration on a straight line; integration goes the other way.
Constant acceleration is the special case with ready formulas; variable acceleration needs calculus or a = v dv/dx.
Velocity is always tangent to the path, and normal acceleration v²/ρ is the part that changes direction.
Radial-transverse components are the natural choice when the radius and angle both change.
A projectile is two independent straight-line motions: constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration g.
Relative velocity depends on the chosen frame, and a string or contact adds a constraint equation.
Newton's second law holds in an inertial frame, and adding −ma gives D'Alembert equilibrium.
Net work changes kinetic energy, and conservative forces let you trade kinetic for potential energy.
Impulse equals change in momentum, and zero external impulse means momentum is conserved.
In impact, momentum is conserved along the line of impact, while the coefficient of restitution fixes the relative speed after collision.
bank_note: Long answers usually expect a clear free-body or kinematic sketch, a stated sign convention, the governing equation in symbols, and then substitution, with special attention to projectile trajectory, normal-tangential acceleration, D'Alembert equilibrium, work-energy and impulse-momentum impact problems.

bank.q: Define rectilinear motion. Starting from a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt, derive the three constant-acceleration formulas v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
outline: State sign convention and that a is constant
Integrate dv = a dt with v(0)=u
Integrate dx = v dt with x(0)=0
Eliminate t to get v² relation

bank.q: Explain tangential-normal and radial-transverse components of acceleration in curvilinear motion. Write the formulas for each component and state one situation where each set is convenient.
outline: a_t=dv/dt changes speed; a_n=v²/ρ changes direction
Polar formulas for r and θ
Use normal-tangential for known path, polar for rotating radius

bank.q: State Newton's second law for a particle and D'Alembert's principle. Show with a free-body diagram how the inertia force converts a dynamics problem into a statics problem.
outline: Example block on incline or lift

bank.q: Define coefficient of restitution. Distinguish direct central impact from oblique central impact and state which quantities are conserved in each.
outline: e formula along line of impact
Momentum conserved along line; perpendicular velocity unchanged for smooth bodies

bank.q: A particle moves on a straight line with acceleration a = (6t − 2) m/s². At t = 0, its velocity is 4 m/s and position is 0 m. Find v(t), x(t), and the distance travelled in the first 3 s.
outline: Integrate a to v with constant
Integrate v to x with constant

bank.q: A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at 30° above horizontal from level ground. Using g = 9.81 m/s², find time of flight, maximum height, horizontal range, and the equation of the trajectory.
outline: Eliminate t to get y = x tanθ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ)

bank.q: Two blocks of masses m₁ and m₂ are connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley, with m₁ on a smooth incline of angle θ and m₂ hanging vertically. Draw free-body diagrams, write the constraint equation, and find the acceleration and string tension.
outline: Newton or D'Alembert equations along motion
Check limiting cases θ=0 and θ=90°

bank.q: A 2 kg particle has initial velocity (3i + 4j) m/s. A force F = (4t i + 6 j) N acts for 3 s. Find the velocity at t = 3 s using the impulse-momentum principle.
outline: Add to initial momentum and divide by mass

bank.q: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall horizontally at 10 m/s and rebounds at 6 m/s. If contact lasts 0.02 s, find the impulse on the ball and the average force by the wall. State the direction.
outline: Take direction away from wall positive

bank.q: A 1 kg collar slides from rest down a frictionless wire from height 2 m and enters a vertical circular loop of radius 0.5 m. Use work-energy to find its speed at the top of the loop and the minimum release height needed to just stay in contact.
outline: Energy at release and at top
At top normal force N + mg = mv²/R

bank.q: A car rounds a horizontal curve of radius 80 m at constant speed 20 m/s. Explain why it has acceleration although its speed is constant. Derive a_n = v²/ρ and discuss the role of friction in preventing skidding.
outline: Derive a_n from similar triangles or calculus

bank.q: Two identical smooth spheres collide obliquely. Given their velocities before impact and e, set up the equations to find the velocities after impact along and perpendicular to the line of impact. Show that kinetic energy is lost when e < 1.
outline: Resolve velocities along and perpendicular to line
Energy loss proportional to (1−e²) relative normal speed

bank.q: A block of mass m rests on a wedge of mass M that can slide on a smooth floor. The block is released from rest on the smooth incline. Derive the constraint relation between block and wedge accelerations, then find the wedge acceleration using Newton's laws.
outline: Result a = mg sinθ cosθ/(M + m sin²θ) for smooth surfaces

bank.q: Compare the work-energy and impulse-momentum methods for a particle under a time-dependent force. For a force F = kt acting from rest, find velocity and displacement at time t by both methods and explain when each method is shorter.
outline: Work: integrate F dx with v(t)
Work-energy needs force as function of position or v

glossary.def: A body whose size and shape are ignored and whose mass is treated as concentrated at a point.
A vector from the origin of a chosen frame to the particle; it fixes location in space.
The change in position vector from initial to final point; it is not the same as distance travelled.
The rate of change of position with time; v = dr/dt, a vector tangent to the path.
The rate of change of velocity with time; a = dv/dt, a vector.
Motion with constant velocity on a straight line, so acceleration is zero.
Motion in which velocity changes with time, so acceleration is nonzero.
The radius ρ of the circle that best fits the path at a point; used in a_n = v²/ρ.
The rate of change of angle with time; ω = dθ/dt, measured in rad/s.
The rate of change of angular velocity; α = dω/dt, measured in rad/s².
A coordinate system with a clock from which position, velocity and acceleration are measured.
A frame in which a free particle remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion; Newton's laws hold.
A restriction such as a string, track or contact that limits possible motion and gives a relation between coordinates.
The fictitious force −ma added in D'Alembert's principle to write a dynamics problem as equilibrium.
Energy of motion; K = ½mv² for a particle of mass m and speed v.
Work done by a force is W = ∫F·dr; it is a scalar measured in joules.
A force whose work between two points is independent of the path, so a potential energy can be defined.
Energy stored in a conservative force field by virtue of position; examples are mgh and ½kx².
The sum of kinetic and potential energy of a particle or system.
The time integral of force, J = ∫F dt; it equals the change in linear momentum.
The product p = mv of mass and velocity; a vector conserved when net external impulse is zero.
A number e between 0 and 1 that gives the ratio of relative speed after impact to relative speed before impact along the line of impact.
Impact in which the contact force acts along the line joining the centres of the two bodies.
A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved; e = 1 for direct central impact of smooth bodies.
A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved; e < 1, and e = 0 for perfectly plastic impact.
The common normal at the contact point during impact; momentum is conserved along this line.
